storylines.label: Kimi K3.1
storylines.latest_title: Moore Threads Adds Day-Zero Kimi K3.1 Pro Support on MTT S5000 GPUs

prior_narrative.tldr: Kimi K3.1 surfaced as an unreleased name after Arena testing, then Moonshot launched the roughly 3T-parameter K3.1 Pro on Oct 24. A quota-driven rocky rollout was followed by third-party hosting, vLLM day-0 support and, on Nov 5, full open weights.
prior_narrative.whats_new: vLLM's Nov 6 post uses Kimi K3.1 as a test case for zero-mismatch async RL, aligning rollout and training kernels bit for bit one day after the full weights shipped.
prior_narrative.why_it_matters: K3.1 Pro is now self-hostable on vLLM and Ascend, and vLLM's RL work shows it is also a fine-tuning target. Licence terms and a 1.56TB footprint decide whether that beats third-party hosts or first-party quotas.

status.detail: K3.1 Pro moved from a quota-troubled first-party launch to third-party hosting, vLLM support and a full weights release; vLLM now documents RL training with it. Independent quality and cost data are still thin.

beats.summary: Coverage names the unreleased model and signals an imminent release.

beats.summary: SiliconANGLE reports the launch; Latent Space calls it near closed-model quality with open weights and notes a faster Highspeed API tier.

beats.headline: Quotas reset after user complaints; Moonshot apologises
beats.summary: Users hit quota problems after launch; Moonshot reset the quotas on Oct 26 and apologised and restored them on Oct 27.

beats.headline: NEAR and ZenMux add K3.1 Pro
beats.summary: Third-party platforms list the model, ZenMux for long-context workflows.

beats.headline: vLLM day-0 support and Verda preview
beats.summary: vLLM details sparse attention on a KDA hybrid, a packed KV cache and fused low-latency decode; Verda previews inference with K3.1 Pro.

beats.headline: Full weights published, Huawei Ascend adds day-zero support
beats.summary: Moonshot releases the full 1.56TB, 2.8T-parameter weights with conditional commercial use; Huawei Ascend lists day-zero support.

beats.headline: vLLM applies zero-mismatch async RL to Kimi K3.1
beats.summary: vLLM describes aligning rollout and training kernels and unclipped importance sampling for stale-weight lag, covering DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, Kimi K3.1 and AMD MI355X.

open_questions: Do independent evals show K3.1 Pro matching Opus 5.5 on coding or agent tasks?
What do the commercial-use conditions in the weights licence actually restrict?
What do third-party hosts charge versus Moonshot's first-party plans and quotas?
Does anyone publish a K3.1 RL fine-tune that uses vLLM's zero-mismatch setup?
prior_narrative.take_for_builders: Read the weights licence conditions before planning a self-host, and budget for 1.56TB of storage. Pin the vLLM version and rerun your own evals against Opus 5.5 before changing routing; for RL, check the bit-for-bit kernel alignment in vLLM's post first.

storylines.latest_title: Supercharging XLA-Based Inference: Announcing the Launch of XLA Serving Engine

prior_narrative.tldr: DeepSeek tied its V4.1-Flash model to its own agent harness on Oct 17, then on Oct 20 open-sourced DeepInfer, the inference engine behind its production services. On Oct 31 it published the architecture of an always-on coding agent, dsh-superagent.
prior_narrative.whats_new: Coverage of the dsh-superagent prototype, a router-worker coding agent that watches team chat for work, continued through Nov 4, while the rest of the thread is third-party inference-engine news.
prior_narrative.why_it_matters: DeepSeek is releasing both the serving layer (DeepInfer, reportedly 155T tokens/day) and an agent harness, so platform teams can inspect a production-scale stack, but the cost and throughput figures come from DeepSeek and press reports, not independent benchmarks.

status.detail: Two DeepSeek open-source drops, DeepInfer and dsh-superagent, with no independent benchmarks yet.

storylines.label: Large Language
storylines.latest_title: Show HN: Thinker – Trim context and cache knowledge to extend agent usage limits

prior_narrative.tldr: This thread is a broad reading list on LLM behavior, reliability and knowledge. Oct 16-28 papers covered sycophancy, hallucination, steering and evals, then Mistral Large 4 landed on Hugging Face and vLLM on Oct 29 as work shifted to memory and retrieval.
prior_narrative.whats_new: Nov 2-5: Anthropic reported zkSNARK progress for provable inference, and a Show HN tool, Thinker, trims context and caches knowledge to stretch agent token limits.
prior_narrative.why_it_matters: The practical thread is context cost and knowledge handling: retrieval, memory and context trimming decide agent reliability and token spend more than any single model release here.

beats.headline: Early papers probe sycophancy, code-translation hallucination and search-state awareness
Price comparison, spectral edits, low-resource adaptation and KG-to-text benchmarks
Long-horizon search evals, neuron steering, vulnerability probing, continual learning and translated benchmarks
Mistral Large 4 ships on Hugging Face and vLLM; papers turn to self-learning and memory
Knowledge integration, retrieval harnesses, text-to-SQL, pruning and retrieval-to-parametric memory
Provable inference, context engines, answerability judgments and a token-saving context trimmer

open_questions: Do compiled-knowledge and parametric-memory methods beat plain retrieval on production agent workloads?
Will provable inference become practical for hosted model APIs?
Do Mistral Large 4 serving claims on vLLM hold up in independent benchmarks?
prior_narrative.take_for_builders: If agent token limits bite, measure context trimming and caching against your own eval set before adopting it; treat the preprints and the Show HN tool as unreplicated.

storylines.latest_title: FewStepRL: Fine-tuning Few-step Diffusion Models with Reinforcement Learning

prior_narrative.tldr: Reinforcement Learning is a loose grouping of arXiv agent-RL papers, not one developing story. Since Oct 20 it has collected work on rollout cost, search and RAG agents, and a split over fine-grained credit assignment.
prior_narrative.whats_new: Nov 4: an arXiv study finds multi-turn RL gains for LLM agents depend heavily on sampling breadth K and interaction depth, and Nov 3 adds guidance-stabilization and web-agent RL papers.
prior_narrative.why_it_matters: Agent RL results are sensitive to rollout budget, numerical setup and reward granularity, so a reported gain may not transfer to your harness. All are paper-reported, not production evidence.

status.detail: A loose set of agentic-RL papers; the newest tests what multi-turn RL actually improves.

beats.headline: Rollout budgets and numerical stability set the cost of agent RL
beats.summary: Budget allocation, environment-aware scheduling, BF16 rounding alignment, and a managed SageMaker recipe.

beats.headline: Search, data and RAG agents get RL recipes with self-assessment and calibration
Credit assignment: finer signals help in some settings and hurt in others
beats.summary: Twin-world and token-level credit compete with a video-editing study showing finer credit can fail.

beats.headline: Error-targeted training, co-evolved harnesses and skill routing for tool agents
Neighboring RL work: simulation, robustness, explainability, compression, flow models
Multi-turn RL gains depend on sampling breadth and interaction depth

open_questions: Do the multi-turn RL findings hold when sampling breadth and interaction depth are fixed to your production limits?
Do the credit-assignment findings from video editing hold on text-only tool-use agents?
Do reward-disagreement rollout budgets cut cost on agents outside the MCP benchmark?
Does co-evolving the harness with the policy beat a fixed harness on independent tasks?
prior_narrative.take_for_builders: Before adopting any of these recipes, rerun them at your own sampling breadth and turn limits, and A/B fine-grained credit against episode-level reward; treat all results as unreplicated.
